profiles.name: Anthony Bryant
profiles.description: Anthony Garnet Bryant was a Black Panther Party member from California who hijacked National Airlines Flight 97 from New York to Havana on March 5, 1969, expecting revolutionary asylum. Instead the Cuban government imprisoned him, and he spent roughly the next eleven years in Castro's prisons before being allowed to return to the United States in 1980. He faced federal air-piracy charges on his return and was treated leniently in light of his years in Cuban custody; he became an outspoken anti-Castro activist and told his story in the memoir Hijack! He died in 1999.
profiles.finding: Florida Memory FFL1239 identifies former Panther and Hijack author. Deborah Thomas, June 3 1985, State Archives of Florida. Image download blocked by Cloudflare; rights field blank, no public-domain assumption. Continue acquisition and rights review.

profiles.name: Tom Csekey
profiles.description: Tom Csekey was a U.S. Navy enlisted man and a co-founder of GI's Against Fascism, the first antiwar and resistance group organized within the U.S. Navy during the Vietnam War. Formed at San Diego in 1969 out of sailors' grievances over living conditions and institutional racism, the group published the underground newspaper Duck Power and later merged with antiwar marines to form the Movement for a Democratic Military. Csekey was arrested for distributing a banned publication and tried by summary court-martial; convicted, he was demoted in rank and sentenced to twenty days of hard labor in the Navy brig, then transferred to Yuma, Arizona. He ultimately received an honorable discharge.

profiles.name: Raymond Johnson
profiles.description: Raymond Johnson Jr. was a 20-year-old Black nationalist and former Southern University student when he diverted National Airlines Flight 186 to Havana on November 4, 1968. He said he was fleeing racist persecution and fabricated arson accusations in Louisiana. Johnson spent the first four of his eighteen years in Cuba in a Cuban prison. Cuba returned him to the United States on September 11, 1986, and the FBI arrested him at Miami International Airport. He pleaded guilty to kidnapping in exchange for dismissal of the aircraft-piracy count and received 25 years, but the Fifth Circuit vacated that sentence and ordered resentencing because the judge had relied on unsupported allegations. The reviewed sources do not establish his later sentence or release date.

profiles.name: Buddy Shaw
profiles.description: Buddy Shaw was a U.S. Army soldier and one of the "Presidio 27" — the stockade prisoners at the Presidio of San Francisco who, on October 14, 1968, staged a sit-down protest against brutal conditions and the killing of a fellow prisoner, Richard Bunch, who had been shot in the back by a guard three days earlier. Singing "We Shall Overcome" and reading out a list of grievances, the men were charged with mutiny, a capital offense. On appeal in June 1970 the mutiny convictions were reduced to willful disobedience, and the defendants were released after about eighteen months.
profiles.finding: Presidio history found; Air Force Colonel Norman Buddy Shaw not established as same person.

profiles.name: Walter Pawlowski
profiles.description: Walter Pawlowski was a U.S. Army soldier and one of the leaders of the "Presidio 27" stockade protest of October 14, 1968, at the Presidio of San Francisco. During the sit-down — sparked by a guard's killing of the prisoner Richard Bunch — Pawlowski read aloud the protesters' list of grievances. Charged with mutiny, a potential capital offense, he escaped from the stockade on Christmas Eve 1968 together with Keith Mather and fled to Canada.

profiles.name: Ronald Bridgeforth
profiles.description: Ronald Bridgeforth was a Black Panther Party member in San Francisco who spent more than forty years underground. In September 1968 he was arrested after a confrontation with police at a White Front discount store in San Francisco and pleaded guilty to assault with a deadly weapon; in 1969, rather than face sentencing, he fled and disappeared. Living under the name Cole Jordan, he earned bachelor's and master's degrees, raised a family, and worked for years as a community-college counselor in Michigan. In January 2007 he was charged in absentia as the ninth defendant in the San Francisco 8 case — the revived prosecution of former Panthers over the August 29, 1971 shotgun killing of SFPD Sergeant John Young at Ingleside station — while the eight others were arrested across the country. After the SF8 case largely collapsed, Bridgeforth surrendered voluntarily in San Francisco in November 2011, telling the press he had come back to account for his past and live openly. The murder charge was not pursued; he pleaded guilty to the 1968 assault charge and in March 2012, at age 67, was sentenced to a year in county jail. Reconstructed from coverage of the 2007 San Francisco 8 arrests and his 2011 surrender.

profiles.name: Bruce Beyer
profiles.description:
Bruce Beyer (1948-2019) was a Buffalo antiwar organizer and draft resister associated with the Buffalo Nine. Federal agents arrested him during the August 19, 1968 sanctuary protest at Buffalo's Unitarian Universalist Church. He received a three-year sentence in 1969 for assault-related charges arising from the confrontation, then went into exile in Canada and Sweden.

He returned to the United States in October 1977 with former Attorney General Ramsey Clark supporting his case. In his own retrospective account, Beyer said Judge John Curtin later reduced the sentence to thirty days, credited nineteen days already served in 1970, and required him to serve eleven further days at the Erie County Correctional Facility. Those were separate periods of confinement; the years abroad were not time in prison. The exact dates of the later eleven-day period remain unresolved.
profiles.finding: Buffalo University profile, Commons arrest image and Buffalo News obituary found; subject isolation and rights review pending.
